pages.task: A motor casing's temperature readings go up to 64 °C, and the temperature axis has 10 squares. How many °C should each square be?
pages.why: 64 ÷ 10 = 6.4, so each square must be at least 6.4 °C, and the next easy step up is 10 °C. Then 10 squares reach 100 °C, so every reading fits.

pages.name: Below zero
pages.task: A freezer is warming after a power cut. Drag the point to its reading of −10 °C at 4 h.
pages.why: 4 h is 4 squares along. −10 °C is below zero, and each square is 5 °C, so it is 2 squares down, the point (4, −10).

pages.task: Here are the motor's readings, at 10 °C a square. What should you draw through them?
pages.why: The readings rise fast and then level off, so they bend. One smooth curve runs close to all of them, and a straight line cannot.

pages.alt: A table of a tank cooling: 48 degrees at 0 minutes, 32 degrees at 10 minutes, 24 degrees at 20 minutes, 19 degrees at 30 minutes, 17 degrees at 40 minutes, 16 degrees at 50 minutes. A graph with time in minutes along, 5 a square, and temperature up, 5 degrees a square, from 0 to 50. Six points are plotted: the point 0, 48, the point 32, 10, the point 20, 24, the point 30, 19, the point 40, 17, the point 50, 16. The point at the point 32, 10 is the 10 minutes reading swapped; it belongs at the point 10, 32, on the curve.
